report:
## Short answer: No — corticosteroids reduce mortality risk in a subset of patients, but they don't guarantee survival for all critically ill COVID-19 patients.

**What the strongest evidence shows**

The UK RECOVERY trial, a large randomized controlled trial of over 6,000 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, found dexamethasone reduced 28-day mortality specifically among patients requiring supplemental oxygen or invasive mechanical ventilation — a relative reduction of about one-third in ventilated patients and about one-fifth in those needing oxygen alone (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436). Critically, the same trial found **no mortality benefit — and a possible trend toward harm — in patients not requiring oxygen support**, showing the effect is not universal (https://www.recoverytrial.net/results/dexamethasone-results).

A WHO-coordinated prospective meta-analysis of seven RCTs (published in JAMA) confirmed corticosteroids were associated with lower 28-day all-cause mortality in critically ill COVID-19 patients compared with usual care, but the odds ratio (~0.66) still means a majority of severely ill patients in these trials died despite treatment — it lowers risk, not eliminates it (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279).

A more recent large meta-analysis (NEJM Evidence, 2023) of glucocorticoids in patients *not* requiring oxygen found no benefit and possible harm, reinforcing that benefit is confined to more severe/hypoxic disease (https://evidence.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/EVIDoa2200283).

**Conclusion**

Dexamethasone and similar corticosteroids improve survival odds statistically for patients with severe, oxygen-dependent COVID-19, but they are not a guarantee of survival — many treated patients still die, and steroids show no benefit (or possible harm) in less severe cases. This supports a "no" answer to whether steroids "ensure" survival — they improve probabilities in a defined subgroup, not certainty across the board.
